Introduction

The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) represents a frontier in next-generation therapeutic innovation, yet the structural patterns of technology convergence within this interdisciplinary field remain poorly characterized. This study aims to develop a computational framework for predicting which technology linkages are most likely to strengthen within this convergence landscape, thereby providing a data-driven basis for R&D resource allocation.

Method

Global patent data in the AI-CGT field were collected to construct a time-series heterogeneous network in which International Patent Classification (IPC) codes serve as technology nodes and individual patents as knowledge nodes, capturing co-occurrence, affiliation, and citation relationships among technologies. At the macro forecasting level, a Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (THGNN) was employed for link prediction. The model aggregated multi-hop neighbor information through meta-paths and leveraged Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to capture technological evolution dynamics, with the aim of identifying IPC pairs with the highest future association weights. At the micro-analysis level, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling was applied to patents associated with the core IPC pairs. The optimal number of topics was determined by combining perplexity curves with inter-topic distance visualization to reveal the key technological content of these IPC associations.

Result

The temporal heterogeneous graph neural network model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.7539, Average Precision (AP) of 0.7862, and F1 score of 0.7568 for link prediction. Based on this model, multiple high-confidence convergence pathways were identified, among which the predicted potential for association strengthening between biochemical detection (C12Q1) and neural networks (G06N3) and between genetic engineering (C12N15) and neural networks (G06N3) received the highest prediction scores (0.89 and 0.80, respectively), suggesting that these pairs are likely to constitute the primary axes of technology convergence in this field.

Discussion

The two major convergence directions identified above correspond to the core bottlenecks in CGT clinical translation-namely, the precision and safety of gene editing, and the quality control and efficacy monitoring of therapeutic products. These findings reveal a patent-based convergence landscape in which AI-related patent classifications increasingly co-occur with both detection and therapeutic methods, indicating a trend of AI integration across the diagnostic-totherapeutic continuum at the level of patent disclosures. The identified convergence directions are computational predictions based on patent co-occurrence patterns and carry inherent uncertainty; they represent technology convergence signals rather than confirmed implementation. The "macroprediction- micro-analysis" bi-level framework proposed in this study provides a quantifiable, interpretable, and transferable analytical paradigm for technology opportunity identification in interdisciplinary pharmaceutical research.

Conclusion

This study introduces THGNN into technology opportunity prediction in the AI-CGT convergence field and establishes a complete analytical chain from macro-level association identification to micro-level technology interpretation through LDA topic modeling. The findings offer a data-driven decision-making reference for pharmaceutical companies and research institutions seeking to strategically position their R&D pipelines within complex technology landscapes.

Background

Minimally invasive endodontics requires precise visualization to preserve tooth structure, often relying on indirect vision with a dental mirror-a challenging skill for dental students. Although virtual reality (VR) simulators provide immersive environments for dental training, most existing systems primarily focus on procedural simulation and haptic feedback, with limited capabilities for real-time mirror positioning and indirect visual guidance.

Objective

The aim of this study was to evaluate verbal, visual, and haptic VR-based mirror guidance for indirect vision during minimally invasive endodontic access cavity preparation.

Methods

Eligible fourth-year preclinical dental students were recruited through institutional email invitations and public announcements. A randomized controlled crossover trial was conducted with 30 participants, who completed all VR sessions in a simulation laboratory under direct investigator supervision to ensure standardized implementation of the training protocol. Participants performed simulated maxillary first molar access cavity preparations under 4 VR mirror guidance conditions-verbal guidance, visual guidance, haptic guidance, and no guidance-following a randomized 4 × 4 Latin square sequence with a 48-hour washout period between sessions. The primary outcome was outcome error score. Exploratory secondary outcomes included operating area visibility, operating area obstruction, operator posture error, task completion time, and Virtual Reality System Usability Questionnaire score. Outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models accounting for the crossover design. Estimated marginal mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs and partial eta-squared (ηp2) effect sizes were reported, with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons used to account for multiple comparisons.

Results

Guidance modality significantly affected the primary outcome, outcome error score (F3,84=20.34; P<.001; ηp2=0.421). Compared with no guidance, outcome error scores were significantly lower with verbal (MD -0.50, 95% CI -0.76 to -0.24), visual (MD -0.68, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.42), and haptic guidance (MD -0.63, 95% CI -0.89 to -0.37; all adjusted P<.001). Guidance modality also significantly affected operating area visibility (F3,84=12.31; P<.001; ηp2=0.305). Compared with no guidance, visibility duration was significantly greater with verbal (MD 37.79, 95% CI 11.15-64.43 seconds; adjusted P=.001), visual (MD 59.15, 95% CI 32.51-85.79 seconds; adjusted P<.001), and haptic guidance (MD 31.52, 95% CI 4.90-58.15 seconds; adjusted P=.01). No significant differences were detected for operating area obstruction, operator posture error, task completion time, or usability.

Conclusions

VR-based mirror guidance improved the outcome error score and increased operating area visibility during minimally invasive endodontic access cavity preparation. Verbal, visual, and haptic guidance resulted in fewer outcome errors and greater operating area visibility than no guidance, while no significant differences were detected in other performance measures or usability. These findings demonstrate the potential of diverse feedback modalities to provide effective guidance for indirect vision and inform future development of adaptive VR training systems using 1 or more modalities to suit learner needs.
